rows.stem: Let A be a skew-symmetric matrix of order 3. If \( |A| = x \), then \( (2023)^x \) is equal to :
rows.solution: A skew-symmetric matrix satisfies \( A' = -A \). Taking determinants of both sides and using \( |A'| = |A| \), for order 3 we get \( |A| = |-A| = (-1)^3 |A| = -|A| \), so \( 2|A| = 0 \), i.e. \( |A| = 0 \). (This is the standard fact that every skew-symmetric matrix of odd order is singular.) Hence \( x = 0 \), and \( (2023)^x = (2023)^0 = 1 \). So the value is 1, matching the choice 1.

rows.subtopic: Definite Integrals and the Fundamental Theorem
rows.solution: For \( 0 \le x \le 2 \), the curve \( y = \sqrt{4 - x^2} \) is the part of the circle \( x^2 + y^2 = 4 \) lying in the first quadrant, so the integral is the area of a quarter disc of radius 2, namely \( \frac{1}{4}\pi(2)^2 = \pi \). Formally, substitute \( x = 2\sin\theta \), \( dx = 2\cos\theta\,d\theta \), with \( \theta \) running from 0 to \( \frac{\pi}{2} \): the integral becomes \( \int_{0}^{\pi/2} 4\cos^2\theta\,d\theta = 2\int_{0}^{\pi/2}(1 + \cos 2\theta)\,d\theta = 2\left[\theta + \frac{\sin 2\theta}{2}\right]_{0}^{\pi/2} = 2\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) = \pi \). So the value is \( \pi \).

rows.stem: The direction cosines of vector \( \overrightarrow{BA} \), where coordinates of A and B are \( (1, 2, -1) \) and (3, 4, 0) respectively, are :
rows.solution: The vector \( \overrightarrow{BA} \) runs from B to A, so it is the position vector of A minus that of B: \( \overrightarrow{BA} = (1 - 3)\hat{i} + (2 - 4)\hat{j} + (-1 - 0)\hat{k} = -2\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} - \hat{k} \). Its magnitude is \( \sqrt{(-2)^2 + (-2)^2 + (-1)^2} = \sqrt{9} = 3 \). Dividing each component by the magnitude gives the direction cosines \( -\frac{2}{3}, -\frac{2}{3}, -\frac{1}{3} \). Two checks worth making: the order of the letters matters, since \( \overrightarrow{AB} \) would give the same three numbers with the opposite sign, and direction cosines must satisfy \( l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = \frac{4}{9} + \frac{4}{9} + \frac{1}{9} = 1 \), which rules out the unnormalised choices \( -2, -2, -1 \) and \( 2, 2, 1 \).

rows.subtopic: Equation of a Line in Space
rows.stem: If the point P(a, b, 0) lies on the line \( \frac{x+1}{2} = \frac{y+2}{3} = \frac{z+3}{4} \), then (a, b) is :
rows.solution: Set \( \frac{x+1}{2} = \frac{y+2}{3} = \frac{z+3}{4} = t \), so a general point of the line is \( (2t - 1,\ 3t - 2,\ 4t - 3) \). The point P(a, b, 0) has third coordinate 0, so \( 4t - 3 = 0 \), giving \( t = \frac{3}{4} \). Then \( a = 2\left(\frac{3}{4}\right) - 1 = \frac{3}{2} - 1 = \frac{1}{2} \) and \( b = 3\left(\frac{3}{4}\right) - 2 = \frac{9}{4} - 2 = \frac{1}{4} \). So \( (a, b) = \left(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{4}\right) \).

rows.stem: For any two events A and B, if \( P(\overline{A}) = \frac{1}{2} \), \( P(\overline{B}) = \frac{2}{3} \) and \( P(A \cap B) = \frac{1}{4} \), then \( P\left( \frac{\overline{A}}{\overline{B}} \right) \) equals :
rows.solution: [This question is defective: none of the four printed options is the correct value, and CBSE acknowledged it. The official marking scheme carries no working for this question at all — its entry reads only "One mark should be awarded to everyone who has attempted this question." The correct value is derived below.] From \( P(\overline{A}) = \frac{1}{2} \) and \( P(\overline{B}) = \frac{2}{3} \) we get \( P(A) = 1 - \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{2} \) and \( P(B) = 1 - \frac{2}{3} = \frac{1}{3} \). Then \( P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B) = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{3} - \frac{1}{4} = \frac{6 + 4 - 3}{12} = \frac{7}{12} \). By De Morgan's law \( \overline{A} \cap \overline{B} = \overline{A \cup B} \), so \( P(\overline{A} \cap \overline{B}) = 1 - \frac{7}{12} = \frac{5}{12} \). Therefore \( P\left(\frac{\overline{A}}{\overline{B}}\right) = \frac{P(\overline{A} \cap \overline{B})}{P(\overline{B})} = \frac{5/12}{2/3} = \frac{5}{12} \times \frac{3}{2} = \frac{5}{8} \). The value \( \frac{5}{8} \) is not among the choices \( \frac{3}{8} \), \( \frac{8}{9} \), \( \frac{1}{8} \), \( \frac{1}{4} \). Note that the given data is itself perfectly consistent — \( P(A \cap B) = \frac{1}{4} \) exceeds neither \( P(A) = \frac{1}{2} \) nor \( P(B) = \frac{1}{3} \) — so the fault lies in the list of options, not in the probabilities supplied.

rows.stem: If \( A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \) and \( B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \), then \( B'A' \) is equal to :
rows.solution: Use the reversal law \( (AB)' = B'A' \), which turns the question into a single product. \( AB = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \), so \( B'A' = (AB)' = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \). Multiplying directly gives the same thing: \( B' = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \) and \( A' = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \), whose product is \( \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \). So the required matrix is \( \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \).

rows.stem:
Consider the statement "There exists at least one value of \( b \in \mathbb{R} \) for which \( f(x) = \frac{b}{x} \), \( b \neq 0 \) is strictly increasing in \( \mathbb{R} - \{0\} \)."
State True or False. Justify.
rows.solution: The statement is True. Here \( f(x) = \frac{b}{x} = b\,x^{-1} \), so \( f'(x) = -\frac{b}{x^2} \). Since \( x^2 > 0 \) for every \( x \ne 0 \), the sign of \( f'(x) \) is simply the sign of \( -b \), and it is the same on both sides of the origin. So take any negative b — for instance \( b = -1 \), giving \( f(x) = -\frac{1}{x} \) and \( f'(x) = \frac{1}{x^2} > 0 \). For every \( b < 0 \) we then have \( f'(x) > 0 \) throughout \( (-\infty, 0) \) and throughout \( (0, \infty) \), so f is strictly increasing on each of the two intervals making up \( \mathbb{R} - \{0\} \). At least one such value of b therefore exists, which is exactly what the statement claims, so it is True. [A note on the wording, not a fault in the marking scheme: \( \mathbb{R} - \{0\} \) is not an interval, and "strictly increasing in \( \mathbb{R} - \{0\} \)" is being read in the usual textbook sense of increasing on each interval of the domain, which is the reading the official scheme uses. Under the stricter global reading, that \( x_1 < x_2 \) should imply \( f(x_1) < f(x_2) \) for every pair drawn from the whole set, no value of b works: with \( b = -1 \) we have \( -1 < 1 \) but \( f(-1) = 1 > f(1) = -1 \), because the two branches are separated by the vertical asymptote at \( x = 0 \).]

rows.stem: Find the value of p, so that lines \( \frac{x-1}{-2} = \frac{y-4}{3p} = \frac{z-3}{4} \) and \( \frac{x-2}{4p} = \frac{y-5}{2} = \frac{1-z}{7} \) are perpendicular to each other.
rows.solution: Read the direction ratios off each line, taking care with the third fraction of the second line. The first line \( \frac{x-1}{-2} = \frac{y-4}{3p} = \frac{z-3}{4} \) is already in standard form, with direction ratios \( \langle -2,\ 3p,\ 4 \rangle \). In the second line \( \frac{1-z}{7} = \frac{-(z-1)}{7} = \frac{z-1}{-7} \), so it reads \( \frac{x-2}{4p} = \frac{y-5}{2} = \frac{z-1}{-7} \) and its direction ratios are \( \langle 4p,\ 2,\ -7 \rangle \); rewriting that fraction is the step this question is really testing, since reading the coefficient as \( +7 \) changes the answer. Two lines are perpendicular when the dot product of their direction ratios vanishes: \( (-2)(4p) + (3p)(2) + (4)(-7) = 0 \), that is \( -8p + 6p - 28 = 0 \), so \( -2p = 28 \) and \( p = -14 \).

The numerator \( e^x \) is exactly the derivative of \( e^x \), which invites the substitution \( t = e^x \), so that \( dt = e^x\,dx \) and \( e^{2x} = t^2 \). The integral becomes \( \int \frac{dt}{\sqrt{t^2 - 4t - 5}} \). Complete the square in the radicand: \( t^2 - 4t - 5 = (t - 2)^2 - 4 - 5 = (t - 2)^2 - 3^2 \). This is now the standard form \( \int \frac{du}{\sqrt{u^2 - a^2}} = \log\left|u + \sqrt{u^2 - a^2}\right| + C \) with \( u = t - 2 \) and \( a = 3 \), giving \( \log\left|(t - 2) + \sqrt{t^2 - 4t - 5}\right| + C \). Substituting \( t = e^x \) back, the answer is \( \log\left|e^x - 2 + \sqrt{e^{2x} - 4e^x - 5}\right| + C \).

rows.subtopic: Graphical Solution and the Feasible Region
rows.stem:
Solve the following linear programming problem graphically :
Maximize z = 3x + 9y
subject to the constraints
\( x + y \geq 10 \),
\( x + 3y \leq 60 \),
\( x \leq y \),
\( x \geq 0 \), \( y \geq 0 \).
rows.solution: Draw the boundary lines \( x + y = 10 \), \( x + 3y = 60 \) and \( y = x \) together with the axes, and shade the region satisfying all five constraints. It is a bounded quadrilateral with vertices A(0, 20), B(0, 10), C(5, 5) and D(15, 15), obtained as follows: the line \( x = 0 \) meets \( x + y = 10 \) at (0, 10) and \( x + 3y = 60 \) at (0, 20); \( y = x \) meets \( x + y = 10 \) at \( 2x = 10 \), i.e. (5, 5); and \( y = x \) meets \( x + 3y = 60 \) at \( 4x = 60 \), i.e. (15, 15). Now evaluate \( z = 3x + 9y \) at each corner: at A(0, 20), \( z = 0 + 180 = 180 \); at B(0, 10), \( z = 0 + 90 = 90 \); at C(5, 5), \( z = 15 + 45 = 60 \); at D(15, 15), \( z = 45 + 135 = 180 \). The largest of these is 180, so the maximum value of z is 180. Because the maximum is attained at two adjacent corners, it is attained at every point of the segment joining them, and the reason is visible in the objective function itself: along AD the constraint \( x + 3y = 60 \) holds, and \( z = 3x + 9y = 3(x + 3y) = 3(60) = 180 \) identically there. So the maximum value is \( z = 180 \), occurring at every point of the line segment AD.

Write \( I = \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \frac{\sin^{100} x}{\sin^{100} x + \cos^{100} x}\,dx \). Replacing x by \( -x \) leaves both \( \sin^{100} x \) and \( \cos^{100} x \) unchanged, because the exponent is even, so the integrand is an even function and the limits can be folded: \( I = 2\int_{0}^{\pi/2} \frac{\sin^{100} x}{\sin^{100} x + \cos^{100} x}\,dx \). Now apply the property \( \int_{0}^{a} f(x)\,dx = \int_{0}^{a} f(a - x)\,dx \) with \( a = \frac{\pi}{2} \), which interchanges sine and cosine: \( I = 2\int_{0}^{\pi/2} \frac{\cos^{100} x}{\cos^{100} x + \sin^{100} x}\,dx \). Adding these two expressions for the same I, the numerators combine to the common denominator: \( 2I = 2\int_{0}^{\pi/2} \frac{\sin^{100} x + \cos^{100} x}{\sin^{100} x + \cos^{100} x}\,dx = 2\int_{0}^{\pi/2} dx = 2\left[x\right]_{0}^{\pi/2} = \pi \). Hence \( I = \frac{\pi}{2} \). Notice the exponent 100 never has to be handled — only the fact that it is even, so the same value would follow for any even power.

rows.stem: Prove that a function f : \( [0, \infty) \to [-5, \infty) \) defined as \( f(x) = 4x^2 + 4x - 5 \) is both one-one and onto.
rows.solution: One-one: let \( x_1, x_2 \in [0, \infty) \) with \( f(x_1) = f(x_2) \). Then \( 4x_1^2 + 4x_1 - 5 = 4x_2^2 + 4x_2 - 5 \), so \( 4(x_1^2 - x_2^2) + 4(x_1 - x_2) = 0 \). Dividing by 4 and factorising, \( (x_1 + x_2)(x_1 - x_2) + (x_1 - x_2) = 0 \), that is \( (x_1 - x_2)\left[(x_1 + x_2) + 1\right] = 0 \). The second factor cannot vanish: since \( x_1 \ge 0 \) and \( x_2 \ge 0 \) we have \( x_1 + x_2 + 1 \ge 1 > 0 \), so the possibility \( x_1 + x_2 = -1 \) is rejected. Hence \( x_1 = x_2 \), and f is one-one. The restriction of the domain to \( [0, \infty) \) is what makes this work — on the whole of \( \mathbb{R} \) this parabola is not one-one, since its vertex sits at \( x = -\frac{1}{2} \). Onto: take any \( y \in [-5, \infty) \) and try to solve \( f(x) = y \), i.e. \( 4x^2 + 4x - 5 - y = 0 \). By the quadratic formula, \( x = \frac{-4 \pm \sqrt{16 + 16(5 + y)}}{8} = \frac{-4 \pm 4\sqrt{6 + y}}{8} = \frac{-1 \pm \sqrt{6 + y}}{2} \). Since \( y \ge -5 \) we have \( 6 + y \ge 1 \), so \( \sqrt{6 + y} \) is real and at least 1. Taking the positive sign gives \( x = \frac{-1 + \sqrt{6 + y}}{2} \ge \frac{-1 + 1}{2} = 0 \), so this x lies in the domain \( [0, \infty) \) and satisfies \( f(x) = y \). (The negative sign would give \( x \le -1 \), outside the domain, so it is discarded.) Every element of the codomain thus has a pre-image, so the range equals the codomain \( [-5, \infty) \) and f is onto. Being both one-one and onto, f is a bijection.
